identity_review.metadata_basis: Two original publisher article routes with identical text, separate correction HTML, article-linked license deed and specified methods/disclosure/source-use sections; completed main 21/13/6 review.
metadata_limits: Both selected URLs return the same article text despite different slash encodings. Retain both stable IDs, recorded labels and five occurrences; the two routes are not independent studies.

One active-release source label names the PLOS article, a separate Norman Mukasa work and a Ugandan MWE/NFA Echuya plan but links only PLOS. Typed metadata here applies only to the linked article. Saved source-review locators identify separate Deusto and ministry URLs; those works are not newly opened or certified in this pass. Preserve the combined historical label and offer a fuller PLOS-only citation for later display.

Original article publication is 16 August 2023, volume 3 issue 8, e0002129. The separate staff correction was published 14 September 2023, volume 3 issue 9, e0002413, and reports republication on 21 August solely to correct title capitalization. Keep the corrected title and all three date roles. The paired original/corrected PDFs linked by the notice were not downloaded or compared; the scope is the publisher’s statement, not a byte-level version audit.

This Batwa-led qualitative study reports purposively recruited adult participants, interviews in Rukiga during August–November 2022, English translation and thematic analysis. Results describe 19 interviews: nine male and ten female participants, aged 21–107. These are study-sample counts, not the population evicted in 1991. The Limitations section explicitly restricts representativeness and transferability beyond the sampled district/community context.

Recruitment and analysis lists repeat a born-after phrase while parenthetically describing young people present at eviction. The Results section clearly distinguishes eleven participants who lived in the Forest as adults, five as young people and three born after eviction. Preserve this textual discrepancy; do not silently rewrite source wording or treat all 19 as adult eyewitnesses in 1991.

The article gives author affiliations and a positionality statement, identifies Wellcome Trust grant 220767/Z/20/Z to Samrawit Gougsa, states the funder had no role, and declares no competing interests. It states ethics approvals and restricts data access pending additional Indigenous ethics agreements. These are author/publisher disclosures, not independently audited funding, ethics, neutrality or dataset validation; no data request was sent.

The abstract places forced eviction with national-park establishment in 1991; Results attribute memories or stories of armed removal and ongoing exclusion to interviewees. This supplies a bounded source-use check, not a new complete event, legal, clinical or causal audit. Narrated illness, mortality and loss are not converted into measured population rates. Wishes for Landback and return are not evidence of a completed return.

The accepted model event is the 1991 Bwindi–Mgahinga unit and explicitly excludes Echuya. Exact gazettement dates and the Echuya institutional distinction rely on the saved multi-source review, including the separate Mukasa and government-plan works. This PLOS metadata review does not independently re-prove those boundaries, reactivate the older umbrella or authorize atlas rendering.

The article concerns the Batwa as people displaced by conservation enforcement. Their displacement or later movement does not establish refugee/flight origins for the incoming state authorities or automatically assign the incoming-flight feature. No score, family, event boundary or flight classification changes.
identity_review.source_passage_scope: Abstract, methods, selected Results and Limitations compared with saved source use. Complete article, underlying data, paired version PDFs and other works in the combined historical label were not newly reviewed.

The publisher-distributor’s indexed Érudit cover explicitly gives DOI 10.7202/1062474ar, Cape Breton University Press, print ISSN 1718-1259, digital ISSN 1927-9264, and rights reserved to Nicolas Landry in 2019. The journal history confirms Cape Breton production from 2006 and a later move to Mount Allison in December 2020; the current institutional home is not backdated to this issue.

Landry reports examining 43 personal files in the Ministry’s series E and explicitly says these cover more than 43 individuals, especially families. The files concern petitioners seeking royal assistance and other claims. They are not a complete deportee census, household roster, property-loss inventory or neutral sample of every refugee.

Printed p.57 describes supplies for ships carrying Miquelon inhabitants to France after the 1778 conquest. Printed p.61 n.23 identifies Saint-Pierre/Miquelon inhabitants sent back to France and receiving subsistence at Cherbourg during 1778–1779. Laroche’s 11,332-livre losses and some other losses discussed on p.57 belong to 1758; they are not reassigned to the 1778 operation.

Printed p.57 says the Ross/Herpin family wished to re-establish itself at Saint-Pierre in 1783 and describes a family of fourteen. This is a particular intention, not a complete actual-return count or census. The current 1778 case already defines the endpoint as restoration and permitted return, preserving this limit.

Printed p.48 and the landing abstract give 1791 for the second conquest. The current second case explicitly discloses that statement and keeps 1793 based on its other accepted sources. Those other works are not newly opened or re-verified in this metadata review; their existing decision is preserved.

The article follows refugees from French colonial communities, with prior flight, residence and proposed re-establishment across distinct periods. This does not establish a flight motive for the British actors in the two current removal cases or justify an automatic incoming-flight flag. Footnote 24 and p.64 point to Mouhot’s separate 2012 Acadian migration study; that work is not opened or newly accepted here.

The article page identifies Landry’s Université de Moncton affiliation and author biography. The journal describes its articles/reports as refereed and assigns responsibility for contributions to their authors; this is a journal self-description, not inspected peer-review records or proof of neutrality. The Érudit direct PDF attempt returned an anti-bot challenge, and the Crossref web URL was rejected as unsafe/non-retryable; neither was bypassed or relabelled successful. Field study ran February–June 2013, combining desk review and interviews in Mogadishu, Doolow and Hargeisa, plus other informants. The report includes later statistics and 2014 narrative; their dates are distinct from the field study, and every claim is not a direct field observation. The report primarily studies IDPs; fluid population, mixed categories and inconsistent methods limit counts.

Refugee in Somalia, Somali refugee and returnee have explicitly stated report-specific meanings. The account of Somaliland administrative practice and state terminology is not a new legal-status ruling. Displacement victims do not automatically establish flight among actors taking land.

PDF 13–16 (printed 10–13) support the national 1991–1995 wave, 1992 peak, 2005–2009 Mogadishu movement, northern front and conflict/land-loss mechanisms at the stated aggregate level. They do not supply individual movement histories, all actors or unique cohorts; drought, famine and violence interact.

PDF 17 and 21 (printed 14 and 18) distinguish reported evictions from public buildings in 2012 and returning-owner removals from the announced January 2013 plan aiming at August 2013 relocation. The plan is not evidence all proposed relocations occurred. General urban trends and late-2013 settlement stocks are not a count of implemented 2012–2013 removals.

PDF 14 describes Puntland independence in 1998 while PDF 15 describes a semi-autonomous declaration in 1993. These are different date and state-status formulations; neither is independently established as corrected history here. PDF 21 lists location counts summing to 149,000 beside 129,400, with footnote 39 identifying unrevised location figures and earlier totals. PDF 22 warns the Somaliland figure excludes some displaced people under local classification. Preserve all denominators and dates; no silent repair.

PDF 21 reports returning refugees and diaspora evicting IDPs; it is a specific lead for incoming-flight research, not a completed flag assignment. PDF 12 and 23–24 distinguish voluntary/coerced return, repatriation pressure, lack of support and plans from outcomes. identity_review.metadata_basis: Two original publisher article routes with identical text, separate correction HTML, article-linked license deed and specified methods/disclosure/source-use sections; completed main 21/13/6 review.
metadata_limits: Both selected URLs return the same article text despite different slash encodings. Retain both stable IDs, recorded labels and five occurrences; the two routes are not independent studies.

One active-release source label names the PLOS article, a separate Norman Mukasa work and a Ugandan MWE/NFA Echuya plan but links only PLOS. Typed metadata here applies only to the linked article. Saved source-review locators identify separate Deusto and ministry URLs; those works are not newly opened or certified in this pass. Preserve the combined historical label and offer a fuller PLOS-only citation for later display.

Original article publication is 16 August 2023, volume 3 issue 8, e0002129. The separate staff correction was published 14 September 2023, volume 3 issue 9, e0002413, and reports republication on 21 August solely to correct title capitalization. Keep the corrected title and all three date roles. The paired original/corrected PDFs linked by the notice were not downloaded or compared; the scope is the publisher’s statement, not a byte-level version audit.

This Batwa-led qualitative study reports purposively recruited adult participants, interviews in Rukiga during August–November 2022, English translation and thematic analysis. Results describe 19 interviews: nine male and ten female participants, aged 21–107. These are study-sample counts, not the population evicted in 1991. The Limitations section explicitly restricts representativeness and transferability beyond the sampled district/community context.

Recruitment and analysis lists repeat a born-after phrase while parenthetically describing young people present at eviction. The Results section clearly distinguishes eleven participants who lived in the Forest as adults, five as young people and three born after eviction. Preserve this textual discrepancy; do not silently rewrite source wording or treat all 19 as adult eyewitnesses in 1991.

The article gives author affiliations and a positionality statement, identifies Wellcome Trust grant 220767/Z/20/Z to Samrawit Gougsa, states the funder had no role, and declares no competing interests. It states ethics approvals and restricts data access pending additional Indigenous ethics agreements. These are author/publisher disclosures, not independently audited funding, ethics, neutrality or dataset validation; no data request was sent.

The abstract places forced eviction with national-park establishment in 1991; Results attribute memories or stories of armed removal and ongoing exclusion to interviewees. This supplies a bounded source-use check, not a new complete event, legal, clinical or causal audit. Narrated illness, mortality and loss are not converted into measured population rates. Wishes for Landback and return are not evidence of a completed return.

The accepted model event is the 1991 Bwindi–Mgahinga unit and explicitly excludes Echuya. Exact gazettement dates and the Echuya institutional distinction rely on the saved multi-source review, including the separate Mukasa and government-plan works. This PLOS metadata review does not independently re-prove those boundaries, reactivate the older umbrella or authorize atlas rendering.

The article concerns the Batwa as people displaced by conservation enforcement. Their displacement or later movement does not establish refugee/flight origins for the incoming state authorities or automatically assign the incoming-flight feature. No score, family, event boundary or flight classification changes.
identity_review.source_passage_scope: Abstract, methods, selected Results and Limitations compared with saved source use. Complete article, underlying data, paired version PDFs and other works in the combined historical label were not newly reviewed.

metadata_limits: The headline, byline and publication name establish the separate Edna Namara news article. Preserve the older title with its parenthetical publication name and the stable ID as provenance.

Displayed publication date is 21 March 2022; embedded publication timestamp agrees. Embedded modification is 10 April 2022. No visible change log or earlier-byte comparison establishes the substance of that modification. Relative last August is read in the 2022 reporting context, not as a fresh legal development.

Edna Namara is credited as reporter and photographer; the article says she translated some interviews from Rufumbira. It also names six editorial roles. These are publisher credits, not proof of independently audited editorial practice, current employment, or accuracy of unseen original interviews.

The article reports an August court victory and a direction to provide land/compensation, but also an appeal, counsel’s expectations of delay, a wildlife-authority response and an implementation warning. Treat these as March 2022 reporting, not an inspected judgment/order, a current appeal outcome or evidence that restitution was completed.

About 200 describes the Rokeri settlement at reporting time, about 6,700 describes Uganda’s Batwa, and more than 200,000 concerns several countries and displacement causes. None is a verified 1991 Bwindi/Mgahinga or Echuya eviction cohort. Ancient-origin and gorilla-population claims were not independently researched or imported into the atlas.

The story mentions three protected areas together and reports Serutokyi’s Echuya connection. This does not establish a common eviction instrument/date or resolve the separately retained Echuya source question.

Speakers’ accounts, wishes for cultural access and the claim that most do not seek permanent return retain speaker and reporting-time attribution. They do not establish a representative preference survey, consent to eviction or completed return. Photographic captions were read; photographs/graphic were not independently inspected here.

Forest Peoples Programme is described as funding the organization’s legal representation, not funding this article. Advocacy organizations, government spokesperson, counsel and community representatives retain their distinct roles. No article funding/conflict disclosure, republishing license or exhaustive institutional audit is asserted.
The comparison with refugees describes displaced Batwa’s hardship; it is not proof that incoming colonizers or conservation authorities were fleeing. No incoming-flight flag is assigned.

A search of the judiciary-associated ULII catalogue returned two similarly titled entries dated 19 August 2021, with conflicting petition-year/citation metadata: UGCC 25 / petition 3 of 2013 and UGCC 22 / petition 3 of 2011. These are leads for a separate primary-document comparison, not accepted judgment identity, duplicate detection or legal holding. No judgment PDF was opened in this article pass.

The print editions and Latin manuscript/critical text were not inspected.

Section 7, Saxon War, reports removal of ten thousand people described as living by the Elbe and settlement with wives and children in scattered groups in Gaul and Germany; [804] is bracketed in this English presentation. The source-attributed number is not an independently checked census or a count of complete households. This passage does not establish the Obodrite land grant, later reversal or c.811 return in the broader event. Those depend on the event’s other sources.

The common site creation 26 January 1996 and latest revision 28 August 2026 are template/design dates. They are not publication dates of every selected page. Einhard’s document notice separately gives August 1996 and January 1999; Appian’s notice gives May 1998. Print-source years 1880 and 1907 have distinct roles. Fordham provides web/server support; the page explicitly calls IHSP independent of Fordham and does not make the university publisher of the ancient or medieval text.

Einhard’s preface claims personal knowledge, court friendship and an obligation to commemorate Charlemagne; his Saxon-war language is overtly partisan. Appian’s transmitted rhetoric concerning slaves, wealth and political factions remains attributed to the text. Host support and contributor credits are disclosed; no exhaustive funding, conflicts or neutrality audit is claimed. Modern electronic-use notices remain distinct from the age of an underlying translation. Raw source evidence remains private.

All three IDs, original labels/URLs and nine occurrences remain. The index has no current citation or case; Einhard binds a release event but no current registry citation. The files concern petitioners seeking royal assistance and other claims. They are not a complete deportee census, household roster, property-loss inventory or neutral sample of every refugee.

Printed p.57 describes supplies for ships carrying Miquelon inhabitants to France after the 1778 conquest. Printed p.61 n.23 identifies Saint-Pierre/Miquelon inhabitants sent back to France and receiving subsistence at Cherbourg during 1778–1779. Laroche’s 11,332-livre losses and some other losses discussed on p.57 belong to 1758; they are not reassigned to the 1778 operation.

Printed p.57 says the Ross/Herpin family wished to re-establish itself at Saint-Pierre in 1783 and describes a family of fourteen. This is a particular intention, not a complete actual-return count or census. The current 1778 case already defines the endpoint as restoration and permitted return, preserving this limit.

Printed p.48 and the landing abstract give 1791 for the second conquest. The current second case explicitly discloses that statement and keeps 1793 based on its other accepted sources. Those other works are not newly opened or re-verified in this metadata review; their existing decision is preserved.

The article follows refugees from French colonial communities, with prior flight, residence and proposed re-establishment across distinct periods. This does not establish a flight motive for the British actors in the two current removal cases or justify an automatic incoming-flight flag. Footnote 24 and p.64 point to Mouhot’s separate 2012 Acadian migration study; that work is not opened or newly accepted here.

The article page identifies Landry’s Université de Moncton affiliation and author biography. The journal describes its articles/reports as refereed and assigns responsibility for contributions to their authors; this is a journal self-description, not inspected peer-review records or proof of neutrality. Original PDF and landing both returned HTTP200. The Érudit direct PDF attempt returned an anti-bot challenge, and the Crossref web URL was rejected as unsafe/non-retryable; neither was bypassed or relabelled successful. Four PDF pages, the landing and listed web-result portions were inspected; the full article, original archives and exhaustive funding/conflict history were not.

Current-host eISSN 2603-6002 is separately labelled; neither it nor the later journal name is backdated as the original 2012 imprint.

The abstract and pp.72–73 describe a three-stage literature review drawing on published/unpublished work, reports, legal documents and other sources. It is not a newly conducted interview study or a primary household census. Its cited official instruments and empirical studies were not independently reopened here.

Figure 1 is on printed p.73 (PDF page 3) and places the parks and Echuya reserve in geographic context. Section 1.5 begins on p.77, and Table 1 is on p.78 (PDF page 8). Table 1 reports an earlier May 1991 Mgahinga resolution and a 13 August 1991 Bwindi resolution. These are source-reported gazettement dates, not verified uniform eviction days for every household.

The 1991 row of Table 1 reports eviction and restriction without resettlement or compensation. The surrounding pp.78–79 separately discuss later trust funding and selective compensation; the article says the fund began operating in 1995. The event-time absence is not expanded into a claim that no later assistance or compensation existed for anyone. The underlying resolutions, compensation ledgers and uniform household chronology remain uninspected.

A location map showing Echuya near the parks does not make it part of the same legal or administrative eviction event. Preserve the accepted Bwindi–Mgahinga unit and separate Echuya boundary. The latter’s detailed institutional chronology still depends on the separately cited government plan and prior source review; that plan was not newly retrieved in this pass.

The article identifies Mukasa as a Deusto PhD candidate and thanks Felipe Gómez and Leslie Lieberman for guidance and encouragement; these are historical source statements, not a claim about his current employment. The journal’s current page names an institute sponsor and Basque/University supporters, which are not automatically assigned as this 2012 article’s funders. The World Bank/GEF fund discussed on pp.78–79 concerns the conservation project, not publication funding. No exhaustive article funding/conflict or peer-review audit is claimed.

The review concerns Batwa removal, forest exclusion and aftermath. It does not establish flight/refugee origins for the conservation authorities or justify an incoming-flight flag. No event admission, family, score, map or flight classification changes.

typed_fields.title: Periochae
typed_fields.source_work_title: History of Rome since the Foundation
typed_fields.source_type: ancient historical epitome in English translation

passage_rule: Occurrence titles and source locators are retained separately. No edition, translator or passage is inferred from a host name.

identity_review.metadata_basis: SOURCE_OBSERVATIONS.json, GROUNDING_PASSAGES.json and completed main 21/13/6 rounds.
metadata_limits: The selected page covers summaries 51–55. Section 53.1 reports Appius Claudius’s subjugation of the Salassians; its displayed bracketed 143 date is separate from the translated clause. This does not itself document Eporedia’s foundation, land parcels, expelled numbers or the whole 143/140–100 sequence. The frozen event cites a broader bundle and already distinguishes the chronology question. Other summaries’ population and battle numbers do not migrate into this event.

Livy is identified as the author of the underlying history, not silently credited as the maker of the Periochae. The explanatory page distinguishes maker/epitomator, reports differences in sequence and missing summaries, and calls Lendering’s translation rather free. Andrew Smith is thanked for suggested improvements, not named as co-translator. The maker and underlying Latin edition remain unverified. The page’s speculative explanation for summary shortening is not adopted.

The displayed bodies are English translations. The site’s Greek labels for Appian/Philostratus and Latin label for Livy refer to the ancient source language. No Greek or Latin critical text was inspected in this pass.

Page creation years 2005, 1998 and 2009 and explicit modification dates in 2020 are website dates. Conybeare 1912 is a credited Loeb translation year. The Horace White printing/year is not supplied. Modern page dates, ancient narrative chronology, copyright range and access date remain separate.

Three original URLs and seven occurrences remain distinct. The Periochae HTML contains span id 53.1 immediately beside the Salassian clause; a more specific label/fragment is offered, not required. No browser jump or highlight behavior was tested. Appian’s displayed 1.c is the passage referred to conventionally as 1c in the note.

About describes Livius as written/maintained by Jona Lendering since 1996 and not for profit, with reuse conditions and exceptions. FAQ solicits financial support. These are the site’s statements; no independent funding audit, donor list, complete rights review or competing-interest determination was performed. No blanket no-funding claim is made.

Ten HTML requests are terminal; thirty private source/derived files are bound. Reading is limited as stated per record. About, FAQ, Appian Histories text, Philostratus introduction, Livy stub and Periochae explanatory text were read in full. The substantive Livy biography was only searched/read around the lead. Images, graphs, visual table colors, physical books, complete ancient works, external archives and remote backup remain uninspected or incomplete.

identity_review.metadata_basis: Three original HTML sources, selected text ranges, host credits and one preserved Appian comparison; completed main 21/13/6 rounds.
metadata_limits: Appian is the ancient author; Oliver J. Thatcher is the source-anthology editor; J. S. Arkenberg is credited with scanning. The host credits page identifies Jerome S. Arkenberg as a contributing editor for scanning/input, but the typed field retains the local initials. No translator is named on the selected page. Do not inherit Horace White from the distinct Perseus or LacusCurtius editions.

The Fordham paragraph under [For 122–121 B.C.] corresponds to Appian Civil Wars 1.24 in the preserved LacusCurtius source. Both contain six thousand colonists, recruitment from Italy, town/boundary layout and repeal conflict. This is a passage-location comparison of the same ancient account, not independent historical corroboration or proof of exact translation/edition identity. The Fordham footer literal I: I-3 is retained as reported, not read as the entire modern section range.

The existing Junonia citation is already correctly specific; no replacement is required. Neither six thousand households nor equal 200-iugera lots nor a computed footprint follows from Appian. The law’s later protection, transfers and institutional-duration qualifications remain assigned to Kim and legal evidence. No modern resident-removal finding, recruitment route or change of start date follows from the page’s editorial date caption.

The common site creation 26 January 1996 and latest revision 28 August 2026 are template/design dates. They are not publication dates of every selected page. Einhard’s document notice separately gives August 1996 and January 1999; Appian’s notice gives May 1998. Print-source years 1880 and 1907 have distinct roles. Fordham provides web/server support; the page explicitly calls IHSP independent of Fordham and does not make the university publisher of the ancient or medieval text.

Einhard’s preface claims personal knowledge, court friendship and an obligation to commemorate Charlemagne; his Saxon-war language is overtly partisan. Appian’s transmitted rhetoric concerning slaves, wealth and political factions remains attributed to the text. Host support and contributor credits are disclosed; no exhaustive funding, conflicts or neutrality audit is claimed. Modern electronic-use notices remain distinct from the age of an underlying translation. Raw source evidence remains private.

All three IDs, original labels/URLs and nine occurrences remain. The index has no current citation or case; Einhard binds a release event but no current registry citation. Appian binds the existing Junonia citation/case. Reading these passages for source identity and locators does not reopen accepted scientific or authoring decisions, create a hold, or assign flight origin.
